questions.problem: Given that $L\{{t}^{n}\}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}},$ find the Laplace transform $L\{{e}^{-3t}\cdot {t}^{4}\}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$
then
$L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$

Using the given result, we have

$$
L\{{t}^{4}\}=\frac{4!}{{s}^{5}}.
$$

Therefore, applying the first shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{-3t}\cdot {t}^{4}\} & =\frac{4!}{(s+3)^{5}} \\  & =\frac{24}{(s+3)^{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)=3{e}^{t}+4{t}^{2}{e}^{-3t}$  for $s>1.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{3{e}^{t}+4{t}^{2}{e}^{-3t}\} \\  & =L\{3{e}^{t}\}+L\{4{t}^{2}{e}^{-3t}\} \\  & =3L\{{e}^{t}\}+4L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{-3t}\}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{2}\} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$then$L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{-3t}\} & =\frac{2}{(s+3)^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =3L\{{e}^{t}\}+4L\{{t}^{2}{e}^{-3t}\} \\  & =3\cdot \frac{1}{s-1}+4\cdot \frac{2}{(s+3)^{3}} \\  & =\frac{3}{s-1}+\frac{8}{(s+3)^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>1.$

Given that

\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)=t({e}^{2t}-1)$ for $s>2.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{t({e}^{2t}-1)\} \\  & =L\{t{e}^{2t}-t\} \\  & =L\{t{e}^{2t}\}-L\{t\}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t\} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore, 

$$
L\{t{e}^{2t}\}=\frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{t{e}^{2t}\}-L\{t\} \\  & =\frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}}-\frac{1}{{s}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4(s-1)}{{s}^{2}(s-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>2.$

Consider a function $f(t)$ for which the graph of the Laplace transform $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$ is shown above. Which of the following could be the graph of $L\{{e}^{-2t}f(t)\}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$
then
$L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$

This implies that multiplying a function $f(t)$ by ${e}^{at}$ shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the $s$-axis.

- If $a>0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the right.

- If $a<0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of $L\{{e}^{-2t}f(t)\},$ we must shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $2$ units to the left.

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{-5t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}

Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{-5t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{-5t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+5)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $Z(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+5)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t=Z(s+5),
$$

where 

$$
s+5>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}-5.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider a function $q(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L\{q(t)\}=Q(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L\{{e}^{9t}q(t)\}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{9t}q(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,q(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{9t}q(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{9t}\,q(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-9)t}\,q(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $Q(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,q(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-9)t}\,q(t)\,\text{d}t=Q(s-9),
$$

where 

$$
s-9>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}+9.

questions.problem:
Consider a function $h(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L\{h(t)\}=H(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L\{{e}^{5t}h(t)\}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{5t}h(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,h(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{5t}h(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{5t}\,h(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-5)t}\,h(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $H(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,h(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-5)t}\,h(t)\,\text{d}t=H(s-5),
$$

where 

$$
s-5>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}+5.

questions.problem:
Consider a function $n(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L\{n(t)\}=N(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L\{{e}^{-4t}n(t)\}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{-4t}n(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,n(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{-4t}n(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{-4t}\,n(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+4)t}\,n(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $N(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,n(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+4)t}\,n(t)\,\text{d}t=N(s+4),
$$

where 

$$

questions.problem:
Consider a function $u(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L\{u(t)\}=U(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L\{{e}^{-2t}u(t)\}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{-2t}u(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,u(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{-2t}u(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{-2t}\,u(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+2)t}\,u(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $U(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,u(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+2)t}\,u(t)\,\text{d}t=U(s+2),
$$

where 

$$
s+2>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}-2.
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Applying the First Shifting Theorem
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $\mathcal{L} \left\{t\sin(\omega t) \right\}=\dfrac{2\omega s}{(s^2+\omega^2)^2},$ find the Laplace transform $\mathcal{L}\left\{e^{-5t}\cdot t\sin(2t)\right\}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$\mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} = F(s),$
then
$\mathcal{L}\left\{e^{at}f(t)\right\}  = F(s-a).$

Using the given result, we have

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{t\sin(2t) \right\} = \frac{2(2)s}{(s^{2}+2^2)^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, applying the first shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{-5t}\cdot t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\} & =\frac{2(2)(s+5)}{((s+5)^{2}+{2}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4(s+5)}{((s+5)^{2}+4)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Applying the First Shifting Theorem and Linearity
canonical_examples.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of  $g(t) = 2t^2 + 5te^{4t}$ for $s > 4.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{g(t)\} & =L\{2{t}^{2}+5t{e}^{4t}\} \\  & =L\{2{t}^{2}\}+L\{5t{e}^{4t}\} \\  & =2L\{{t}^{2}\}+5L\{t{e}^{4t}\}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s > 0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t\} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}} \\ L\{{t}^{2}\} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $\mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} = F(s),$ then $\mathcal{L}\left\{e^{at}f(t)\right\}  = F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{ te^{4t} \right\} = \dfrac{1}{(s-4)^2}.
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $g(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{g(t)\} & =2L\{{t}^{2}\}+5L\{t{e}^{4t}\} \\  & =2\cdot \frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+5\cdot \frac{1}{(s-4)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{5}{(s-4)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>4.$

Example: 
                    Identifying Graph Shifts From the First Shifting Theorem
canonical_examples.problem: Consider a function $f(t)$ for which the Laplace transform is $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s).$ How can we obtain the graph of $\mathcal{L}\{e^{-6t} f(t)\}$ from the graph of $F(s)?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$\mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} = F(s),$
then
$\mathcal{L}\left\{e^{at}f(t)\right\}  = F(s-a).$

This implies that multiplying a function $f(t)$ by $e^{at}$ shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the $s$-axis.

- If $a > 0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the right.

- If $a < 0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of $\mathcal{L}\{e^{-6t} f(t)\},$ we must shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $6$ units to the left.

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Proving the First Shifting Theorem
canonical_examples.problem: Consider a function $f(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s)$ for $s>s_0.$ Suppose we wish to find $\mathcal{L}\{e^{-7t} f(t)\}.$ Show the steps to compute this transform.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{-7t}f(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{-7t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+7)t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $\displaystyle F(s) = \int_0^{\infty} e^{-st} \, f(t)\, \textrm{d}t,$ where $s > s_0.$ Therefore, 

$$
\int_0^{\infty} e^{-(s+7)t} \, f(t)\, \textrm{d}t = F(s+7),
$$

where 

$$
s + 7 > s_0
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad 
s > s_0 - 7.
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
In a previous lesson, we learned how to compute Laplace transforms. We now examine how the Laplace transform changes when a function is multiplied by an exponential.

Suppose

$$
\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\}=F(s)
$$

exists for $s>s_0.$ We want to compute the Laplace transform of $e^{at}f(t).$

Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform,

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,{e}^{at}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-a)t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now recall that

$$
F(s)=\int_0^{\infty} e^{-st}\,f(t)\,\textrm{d}t,
\qquad s>s_0.
$$

Comparing the two integrals, we see that

$$
\int_0^{\infty} e^{-(s-a)t}\,f(t)\,\textrm{d}t
=F(s-a).
$$

For this to make sense, we need $s-a>s_0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
s>s_0+a.
$$

This result is known as the **First Shifting Theorem**:

$$
\mathcal{L}\{e^{at}f(t)\} = F(s-a).
$$

In the next slide, we will apply this result to a concrete example.

tutorials.name: Using the First Shifting Theorem
tutorials.problem:
The **First shifting Theorem** states that if

$$
\mathcal L\{f(t)\}=F(s)
$$

for $s>s_0$, then

$$
\mathcal L\{e^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a),
\qquad s>s_0+a.
$$

So, when you multiply a function by $e^{at}$, you do two things:

- *Replace* $s$ with $s-a$ in the known transform $F(s)$.

- *Shift the domain* from $s>s_0$ to $s>s_0+a$.

To see this in action, consider the following example.

We are given that

$$
\mathcal{L}\{\sin(\omega t)\}=\frac{\omega}{s^2+\omega^2},
\qquad s>0.
$$

Suppose we want to compute

$$
\mathcal{L}\{e^{2t}\sin(3t)\}.
$$

First, we identify the base transform:

$$
\mathcal{L}\{\sin(3t)\}=\frac{3}{s^2+3^2}
$$

Next, we apply the first shifting theorem with $a=2$, which means we replace $s$ by $s-2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\} & =\frac{3}{(s-2)^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3}{(s-2)^{2}+9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the original transform is valid for $s>0$, the shifted transform is valid for

$$
s>2.
$$

This example illustrates the general pattern: multiplying by $e^{at}$ leads to a simple substitution $s:= s-a$, along with a corresponding shift in the domain.

tutorials.name: Graph Shifting
tutorials.problem:
Recall that the first shifting theorem states that if

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} = F(s),
$$

then

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{e^{at}f(t)\right\}  = F(s-a).
$$

This means the new Laplace transform is the original graph of $F$ evaluated at $s-a$.

So, the graph shift is:

- If $a>0$, then $F(s-a)$ is the graph of $F(s)$ **shifted to the right** by $a$ units.

- If $a<0$, then $F(s-a)$ is the graph of $F(s)$ **shifted to the left** by $|a|$ units.

For example, suppose $F(s)$ has the following graph:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14134507/assets/45ce62c981e4c7853ef158046eb21fbc9c135f5fa0a8887d813a07594077c8ce.png)

Then the Laplace transform of $e^{-3t} f(t)$ is $F(s+3).$ Here, $a=-3$, so this corresponds to shifting the graph of $F(s)$ three units to the left:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14134507/assets/b75658824079fe90c9c4f43d4d37d355c95b845ebed3f11bdf751b52f8d34f55.png)

A useful self-check is that any horizontal features move the same way:

- vertical asymptotes shift left/right by the same amount,

- intercepts and key points shift left/right by the same amount.

tutorials.name: A Laplace Transforms Comparison Table
tutorials.problem:
Using the first shifting theorem, we can obtain new Laplace transforms from old ones without performing any additional integration.

If

$$
\mathcal L\{f(t)\}=F(s)
$$

for $s>s_0$, then

$$
\mathcal L\{e^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a),
\qquad s>s_0+a.
$$

The table below shows some general results we can obtain using the first shifting theorem.

| $f(t)$ | $F(s)=\mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\}$ | Compare With |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $e^{at} t^n$ | $\dfrac{n!}{(s-a)^{n+1}}$ | $\mathcal L \{t^n\} = \dfrac{n!}{s^{n+1}}$ |
| $e^{at}\sin \omega t$ | $\dfrac{\omega}{(s-a)^2+\omega^2}$ | $\mathcal L\{\sin\omega t\} = \dfrac{\omega}{s^2+\omega^2}$ |
| $e^{at}\cos \omega t$ | $\dfrac{s-a}{(s-a)^2+\omega^2}$ | $\mathcal L\{\cos\omega t\} = \dfrac{s}{s^2+\omega^2}$ |

So, each new entry in our table is obtained by taking a known transform and replacing $s$ with $s-a$, and then shifting the domain accordingly.
